analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier for workers to form unions through signed cards instead of elections and tightens penalties on employers who retaliate.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 241-185, but the Senate fell short of the 60 votes needed to even debate it, 51-48, and the bill died.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let workers form a union once a majority signed cards saying so, instead of going through an election employers often contest. It would force employers and a new union into mediation and, if that fails, binding arbitration for a first contract, so a company could not simply stall forever. It would also give fast-track investigations and tougher penalties to workers fired or threatened during union drives. It passed the House but Senate opponents blocked it from ever reaching the floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who want to organize. Under current law, employers can delay union elections for months, campaign against the union, and illegally fire organizers knowing penalties are light. The bill would certify a union as soon as a majority signed cards, set 10 days to start bargaining and a fixed schedule ending in binding arbitration for a first contract, and add up to triple back pay plus fines up to $20,000 per violation for employers who discriminate against workers during organizing campaigns.

how_it_helps.text: The National Labor Relations Board would certify a union without an election whenever a majority of workers in the unit signed authorization cards and no other representative is already recognized.

If a newly certified union and employer cannot reach a first contract, the dispute goes to mediation after 90 days and then to a binding arbitration board whose decision locks in terms for two years, ending open-ended employer delay.
Charges that an employer fired, threatened, or coerced workers during an organizing drive would get priority investigations and could lead to injunctions.

Employers who illegally discriminate against organizing workers would owe back pay plus twice that amount in liquidated damages, and face civil penalties up to $20,000 per willful or repeated violation.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, especially in industries where organizing campaigns are common. Companies could no longer rely on lengthy election delays, would face binding first contracts they did not freely sign, and would face much larger penalties for firing or threatening organizers. The added cost would land partly on their owners and partly, if passed into prices, on consumers.

drawbacks.text: Card-check certification removes the secret-ballot election that currently decides union representation, so a worker signs a card in front of or under pressure from organizers rather than voting privately — the central argument opponents, including the bill's own minority, made against it.

Government-appointed arbitration boards would set the terms of first contracts for two years, meaning wages and conditions at newly unionized workplaces could be decided by an arbitrator rather than negotiated by the parties themselves.
Opponents argued the penalties and expedited procedures applied only to employers, tilting the process toward unions during organizing campaigns.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades one set of bargaining problems for another. It fixes a real, documented problem — employers delaying elections and firing organizers because penalties are too small to matter — but does so by replacing secret-ballot elections with signed cards and by letting arbitrators set first contracts. Workers who want a union gain real leverage; the fairness of the process depends on whether card signing is as free of pressure as a private ballot, which was the crux of the argument against it.

outcome.mechanism: After the House passed it, Senate Republicans filibustered the very motion to begin debating the bill, and with only 51 votes — three short of the 60 needed — it never came up for an up-or-down vote.

narrative.text: The House Education and Labor Committee reported the bill on a 26-19 vote on February 14, 2007, and the full House passed it 241-185 on March 1, 2007, with 228 of 233 Democrats in favor and 13 of 201 Republicans crossing over.
The bill was read in the Senate and placed on the calendar in early March 2007, but it sat there for months with no consideration.
On June 26, 2007, the Senate voted 51-48 on whether to cut off debate on the motion to proceed to the bill; 48 of 49 Republicans voted no, and the motion failed, three votes short of the 60 needed.
Because debate was never allowed to begin, the bill never received an up-or-down vote in the Senate and died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and business groups that campaigned against the bill are better off: the current system of contested elections and light penalties remains in place. Union-backed workers gained nothing from the House win, which produced no law.

for.name: Rep. George Miller
for.role: Chair, House Education and Labor Committee; sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, guided it through committee markup to a 26-19 report, and managed floor passage.

for.name: Rep. Howard McKeon
for.role: Ranking member, House Education and Labor Committee
for.what_they_did: Offered amendments and a motion to recommit requiring proof of citizenship on authorization cards; both failed.

against.name: 48 of 49 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted against cutting off debate on the motion to proceed, denying the bill floor consideration.

against.name: Sen. Arlen Specter
against.role: Senate Republican, the lone crossover vote
against.what_they_did: The only Republican to vote to proceed to the bill.

against.name: U.S. business community
against.what_they_did: Ran a major campaign against the bill, calling card-check an end to the secret ballot and binding arbitration government-imposed contracts.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Administration position opposed the bill; even had the Senate advanced it, a veto was expected.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote was 228-2 among Democrats for and 183-13 against among Republicans; the Senate was near-unanimous by party, with all 48 voting Democrats for and 48 of 49 Republicans against, leaving the bill three votes short of the 60 needed to begin debate.

industries.note: The bill ends their ability to stall elections, refuse first contracts indefinitely, and fire organizers at light penalty. Their interest in defeating it ran against workers' ability to bargain collectively.
Card-check certification would make organizing far faster and cheaper, and binding arbitration guarantees a first contract. Union membership growth is the bill's direct purpose.
